title: Fitting a kitchen worktop post form
subtitle: Measure, cut, and fix a laminate post-form worktop to kitchen base units, including scribing to the wall and mitre joints at corners
excerpt: How to fit a laminate post-form kitchen worktop. Covers setting out and measuring, cutting to length, scribing to an uneven wall, cutting mitres where two runs meet, applying worktop bolts and sealant, and fixing from below.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK kitchen fitting trade practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: A factory-made laminate kitchen worktop with a curved upstand moulded along the back edge and a rounded front nose. It is made from a chipboard core with a heat-bonded laminate surface. Standard depths are 600 mm; standard thicknesses are 38 mm. Cut with a fine-tooth blade on the face-down side to prevent the laminate chipping.

The process of marking and trimming the back upstand of a worktop to follow the exact contour of an uneven wall, so the worktop sits flush against the wall along its full length with no gap. Scribing is done with a pair of compasses set to the maximum gap, drawn along the upstand while the scriber point follows the wall surface.

A knock-down fitting used to draw two lengths of worktop together at a mitre joint. Pairs of bolts are let into pre-routed recesses in the underside of the worktop at the mitre joint, and tightened with a spanner to clamp the joint tight.

content.text: is the most common kitchen top: a laminate-faced chipboard sheet with a built-in curved upstand. The key skills are a clean
to the wall and a tight mitre joint where two runs meet. INTERMEDIATE: the cutting is straightforward; precision in setting out determines the result.

Measure the full length of each worktop run from wall to wall. If the worktop meets a wall at both ends, add the full depth of the return run to the mitre end to allow for the joint. Mark the cut lines with a pencil on the worktop face, checking measurements twice. Mark the line with masking tape on both sides of the cut to reduce laminate chipping.

Cut the worktop face-down with a fine-tooth jigsaw blade to prevent the face laminate chipping. Alternatively, score the face line deeply with a utility knife before cutting. Guide the saw along a straight batten clamped to the worktop, keeping the cut square. Apply iron-on worktop edging strip to any exposed chipboard ends.

Slide the worktop into position with the upstand touching the wall along its full length. Set a pair of compasses to the maximum gap between the upstand and the wall. Draw the compass along the wall, with the point on the wall and the pencil marking the upstand. Trim the upstand along the pencil line with a belt sander or jigsaw to the scribe profile. The trimmed upstand should now follow the wall exactly.
Cut and pull the mitre joint

Most post-form worktops are supplied with pre-cut mitre ends for corner joints. If cutting on site, cut the meeting ends at 45 degrees with the jigsaw, checking the angle against the actual corner of the room. Route or chisel the

recesses in the underside of both pieces at the joint. Apply waterproof PVA or silicone sealant to the mitre faces, bring the joint together, and tighten the worktop bolts progressively to draw the joint tight. Wipe away any sealant squeeze-out from the face immediately.
Fix to the cabinets and seal

Screw up through the corner brackets inside the base cabinets into the underside of the worktop. Use screws no longer than the worktop thickness to avoid breaking through the surface. Apply a continuous bead of silicone sealant between the upstand and the wall tiling, smoothing with a wet finger for a clean line.

attrs.symptom: Gap visible between the upstand and the wall after fitting
attrs.cause: The scribe was not taken to the actual wall profile, or the worktop moved during fixing.
attrs.fix: Fill a small, even gap with a bead of silicone sealant coloured to match the worktop. For a gap wider than 5 mm, remove the worktop and re-scribe.

attrs.symptom: Mitre joint opens slightly on the face after tightening the worktop bolts
attrs.cause: The two mitre cuts are not at exactly the same angle, so the faces do not meet flush along their full depth.
attrs.fix: Adjust one cut with a block plane or belt sander until both faces sit flush. Apply fresh sealant and re-tighten the bolts.
